paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by complete TYK2 deficiency. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype is mycobacterial and/or viral infections, caused by impaired cellular responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta. Affected individuals may have bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) disease, tuberculosis, or other intracellular bacterial infections such as Salmonella and Brucella, as well as herpesvirus and other viral infections.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, the third child of healthy first-cousin parents, who was vaccinated with BCG at 2 months of age. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months, and generalized lymphadenopathy and fatigue followed at 21 months. On admission at 2 years he had fever and fistulous, enlarged bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes. The PPD skin test was negative, and M. bovis BCG was isolated from the draining cervical sinuses. He responded to antimycobacterial treatment without relapse. At 8 years he developed Brucella meningitis with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, after a history of eating unpasteurized cheese. This was followed by severe hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was treated with acyclovir. Serum IgE at 2, 11, 16, and 18 years of age was 80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml, respectively, which was normal or slightly elevated. Serum IgG, IgM, and IgA were normal, but the antibody response to tetanus toxoid was low. He had no atopy, asthma, candidiasis, boils, folliculitis, or cold abscesses, and investigations for skeletal and dental manifestations of HIES were negative. Kilic et al. (2012) contrasted this patient with the Japanese patient of Minegishi et al. (2006), who had severe atopic dermatitis, staphylococcal disease, and a serum IgE of 2,100 IU/ml, but who also lacked the bone fractures and dental and facial features of autosomal dominant HIES.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) gave further clinical details on the Japanese patient (P1) of Minegishi et al. (2006), a man born to consanguineous parents. He had atopic dermatitis from 1 month of age and recurrent bacterial and viral infections from 1 year of age. He developed BCG lymphadenitis at 22 months of age and repeated Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, pneumonia without pneumatocele, otitis, and sinusitis. At 15 years he had sepsis following severe nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis. His viral infections included parainfluenza virus-3 pneumonia, recurrent oral HSV infections with tonsillitis, and molluscum contagiosum, and he also had mild oral candidiasis. Testing repeatedly showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and serum IgE of 1,430 to 2,100 IU/ml. At 30 years of age he had ocular sarcoidosis.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) also reported 7 TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 unrelated families from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. These patients had mycobacterial and/or viral infections but no features of HIES. P2 was the Turkish patient described by Kilic et al. (2012). P3, a Moroccan girl born to first-cousin parents, was hospitalized at 13 years with suspected abdominal tuberculosis. She went on to develop ascites and a psoas abscess from which M. tuberculosis was isolated, and she died of bacterial meningitis 15 months after symptom onset. Her brother (P4) was hospitalized at 8 months for meningitis of unknown etiology. He had recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels. P5, an Iranian boy born to consanguineous parents, developed axillary and cervical lymphadenitis at 2 and 4 months of age after BCG vaccination at birth. At 4.5 years he developed paravertebral and psoas abscesses with fistulization and pulmonary involvement. His younger sister (P6) had BCG lymphadenopathy after vaccination and was hospitalized at 1 year for an unknown viral infection of the skin. P7, a 9-year-old Iranian girl born to consanguineous parents, had miliary tuberculosis with bilateral micronodular lung infiltrates, cavitary consolidation, and hilar, mediastinal, and paraaortic adenopathy. P8, an 11-year-old adopted boy from Argentina, had herpes gingivostomatitis, aseptic herpes meningitis, and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions, as well as mild mental disability that may have been congenital or a consequence of meningitis. None of P2 through P8 had documented pyogenic or staphylococcal infections or fungal infections, and serum IgE was never found to be high. Candidiasis in P1 was limited to a few episodes of mild oral candidiasis.
